background.definition: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is an inherited disorder that primarily affects the kidneys resulting in the formation of multiple fluid filled cysts, along with a variety of extrarenal manifestations. It is broadly divided into two forms: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD).

list.listitem: ADPKD: The point prevalence of diagnosed ADPKD is 2 to 4 per 10,000 persons.
ARPKD: 1 in 20,000 persons
End-stage renal disease (ESRD) due to ADPKD costs an estimated US$1.8 billion per year.
ADPKD accounts for 5% to 10% of cases of renal failure in the US.

ADPKD: Transmission is autosomal dominant and 2 forms occur: 85% of ADPKD cases have mutations of the gene PKD1 located on chromosome 16 (PKD1 form), while 15% of ADPKD cases involve mutations of the gene PKD2 located on chromosome 4 (PKD2 form). PKD1 form is more common and more severe than the PKD2 form.
ARPKD: Transmission is autosomal recessive and involves mutation of the PKHD1 gene located on chromosome 6.

ADPKD: The proteins polycystin 1 and 2 coded by PKD 1 and 2 genes mediate mechanosensation throughout the renal epithelium. An abnormality in polycystin 1 and 2 activity results in an altered reaction of the renal tubular epithelium to mechanical stimuli with resultant cyst formation.

ARPKD: The PKHD1 gene located on chromosome 6p21 codes for a protein named fibrocystin/polyductin localized to renal cilia. Reduced or absent expression of fibrocystin results in cyst formation within the kidney.
Hypertension occurs due to cysts compressing on renal vasculature with resultant renin-angiotensin activation. Pain occurs due to bleeding within cysts, formation of renal calculi and infections.
Consider screening for cerebral aneurysms in patients with a family history of intracranial aneurysms (ICA) in the setting of ADPKD, using MR angiography. B
A systematic review found that they are more likely to be localized in large caliber arteries in the anterior circulation compared with intracranial aneurysms for non-ADPKD patients.
Adults with ADPKD or ARPKD should be informed of the risk of their offspring inheriting the disease. C

Affected individuals and family members should be informed of the risk to their offspring inheriting the disease (for ADPKD, 1 in 2 chance of disease; for ARPKD, 1 in 4 chance of disease and 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier). C
In patients with ARPKD and hypersplenism secondary to portal hypertension consider vaccinations against encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae). C
Ultrasound is the first-line imaging technique recommended in the diagnosis of ADPKD. C
Back and flank pain are the most common symptoms. Other common findings are hypertension, hematuria, UTI and nephrolithiasis. C
Severe hypertension is present in two-thirds of the children early in the course of ARPKD. C

Sonographic diagnostic criteria for individuals older than 15 years of age with a 1 in 2 risk for the disease based on family history include the following: Less than 30 years of age: presence of at least 2 unilateral cysts or bilateral cysts. 30 to 59 years of age: presence of 2 cysts in each kidney. 60 years or older: presence of 4 cysts in each kidney.
Onset of symptoms is typically in the fourth or fifth decade.

Back and flank pain are the most common symptoms and result from cyst hemorrhage, calculi, renal capsule distortion and urinary tract infections. Hematuria occurs in approximately 42% of patients as a result of UTI, cyst rupture, cyst hemorrhage, nephrolithiasis. Polydipsia, polyuria, nocturia may occur due to loss of concentrating ability of the kidneys late in the disease.
Hypertension is present in 49% of patients between 20 and 34 years of age with normal renal function.

Urinary tract infections occur in up to 68% of patients. Pyelonephritis is difficult to distinguish clinically and radiologically from cyst infection. Nephrolithiasis occurs in up to a third of patients. Hepatic manifestations: most liver cysts are asymptomatic, but they can cause symptoms from mass effect.

ICAs occur in 16% of PKD patients with and 6% of patients without a family history of ICAs, respectively. Patients may less commonly develop cardiac valve abnormalities, colonic diverticula, abdominal wall and inguinal hernias.
Depending on the age of presentation, there is marked variability in the clinical presentation and disease course.
Infants and children may present with signs and symptoms due to renal enlargement and ESRD. Severe hypertension is present in two-thirds of children early in the disease course.
Adults may present with manifestations of liver disease, primarily congenital hepatic fibrosis (CHF), hepatic cysts, hepatosplenomegaly, hypersplenism, and cholangitis.

Ultrasound is the first-line imaging technique for diagnosis of ADPKD and ARPKD when clinically suspected (e.g. family history) based on KDIGO guidelines (2025). Sensitivity is somewhat lower in patients under the age of 30 years and in patients with type 2 ADPKD. Therefore, consider genetic testing in addition to ultrasound if there is a clinical suspicion of ADPKD type 2, particularly in individuals younger than 30 years.
In persons with a family history who are aged 16 to 40 years, a cutoff of > 10 cysts on MRI is diagnostic based on KDIGO guidelines (2025) while < 5 cysts excludes the diagnosis.

In patients with incidentally detected cysts consider genetic testing. In patients with few cysts, normal renal function and no extrarenal findings ADPKD is unlikely over the age of 40 years but possible in younger patients.

When ultrasound is equivocal consider further investigation with genetic testing, CT scan, or MRI followed by genetic testing. Genetic testing involves either linkage analysis or direct DNA analysis. PKHD1 mutation screening is a promising diagnostic test in patients suspected with ARPKD.
CT scan and MRI may be more sensitive than ultrasonography. Contrast enhanced CT scanning or MRI or heavy-weighted unenhanced T2 MRI can reliably detect small cysts of 2 to 3 mm diameter.

Ultrasound ARFI elastography of the liver and spleen, particularly of the left liver lobe, is a useful noninvasive biomarker to detect and quantify liver fibrosis and portal hypertension in children with ARPKD.
Suspect PKD in patients with a family history, back or flank pain, or unexplained hematuria; may also be incidental finding on renal imaging. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging technique.
When ultrasound is equivocal, consider further investigation with genetic testing and/or CT scan or MRI.
Consider genetic testing in addition to ultrasound if there is a clinical suspicion of ADPKD type 2 in individuals younger than 30 years.
ACE inhibitors (or ARBs if not tolerated) are preferred for treatment of hypertension in both ADPKD and ARPKD based on expert opinion. C
Effect of ACE inhibitors in slowing progression of kidney disease is inconclusive. B
Tolvaptan is the only drug with good evidence that it slows progression of PKD as measured by eGFR and total kidney volume.C
Patients with ADPKD and T2DM should take metformin and a GLP-1 agonist.B

ACE inhibitors are still preferred as first-line agents in treating hypertension in ADPKD. They provide excellent blood pressure control, reduce proteinuria and have a favorable safety profile. Angiotensin receptor blockers are an alternative if not tolerated.
Effect of ACE inhibitors in slowing progression of kidney disease (ie, doubling of baseline serum creatinine or development of ESRD) is inconclusive.
Management of diabetes in persons with ADPKD should include metformin and a GLP-1 based on KDIGO guidelines (20250.
A Cochrane review concluded that tolvaptan is the only drug with good evidence that it slows progression of PKD as measured by eGFR and total kidney volume. This was also found be another SR.
Patients taking tolvaptain should drink adequate water including skipping doses of tolvaptan on "sick days" when fluid intake is reduced or fluid loss is increased.

The Cochrane review also concluded that targetted low blood pressure results in a small increase in total kidney volume but does not impact other outcomes. Somatostain analogues may decrease total kidney volume but have little effect on eGFR and have significant adverse events. The review also concluded that data regarding choice of antihypertensive agents, mTOR inhibitors, eicosapentaenoic acids, statins, vitamin D, metformin, trichlormethiazide, spironolactone, bosutinib, curcumin, and niacinamide were of poor quality and inconclusive. No intervention, including tolvaptan, has been shown to have an effect on mortality or end-stage renal disease incidence.

A systematic review purported to show that metformin slowed the decline in eGFR. However, the 4 small studies were dominated by a single non-randomized retrospective study, and no benefit seen in the 3 RCTs.
Sirolimus does not inhibit kidney growth or improve renal function. Everolimus slightly improves the rate of kidney growth but does not improve kidney function after 2 years.
Avoid NSAIDs in patients with PKD.

Cyst drainage and decompression are useful for relieving severe or refractory pain in patients with ADPKD, but do not slow down disease progression. The procedure relieves pain in 80% of patients for at least 1 year.

In both ADPKD and ARPKD, dialysis and renal transplantation are options for patients with ESRD. In a series of 565 patients with PKD receiving a transplant, 10 year post-transplant survival was 68% for those receiving transplant alone and 64% for those receiving simultaneous transplant and bilateral nephrectomy. Patients in the latter group also had more renal artery thromboses.
There were no disadvantages associated with simultaneous nephrectomy and transplant compared with staged procedures in a systematic review of 7 retrospective cohort studies.

For patients requiring dialysis, a systematic review of 9 studies with 882 PKD patients concluded that overall they had somewhat lower mortality than the entire population of dialysis patients, with no increase in the risk of peritonitis. The authors conclude that peritoneal dialysis should be an option for these patients.
Low-protein diet showed a small benefit in ADPKD patients with moderate renal insufficiency, but did not significantly slow the progression of the disease in severe renal insufficiency.
Refer to nephrologist to evaluate progression of disease, declining renal function, refractory hypertension, and suitability for renal replacement therapy.
ESRD: Hemodialysis or renal transplant.
Kidney stones: The treatment of nephrolithiasis in patients with ADPKD is not different from that in patients without ADPKD.
Pain control: Control pain with opioid analgesics, acetaminophen or NSAIDS. NSAIDS should be used with extreme caution to avoid precipitation of acute renal failure.
UTI: Use antimicrobial therapy (like fluoroquinolones) to cover Gram-negative enteric organisms.

Infertility: A randomized trial in women with infertility due to PCOS found that frozen-embryo transfer had a higher live birth rate (49% vs 42%, p < 0.001) and less risk of ovarian hyperstimulation than a fresh embryo transfer.
The major cause of death is cardiovascular events. C
Risk factors for ESRD include diagnosis before the age of 30 years, onset of hypertension before the age of 35 years, and gross hematuria before the age of 30 years in men. B

Autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD): Variability in the severity of kidney disease and extrarenal manifestations determine disease course. Average age of onset of ESRD is 56.7 and 69.4 years in patients with PKD1 and PKD2 genotype, respectively. The major cause of death is cardiovascular events.

Autosomal recessive PKD (ARPKD): Depending on the age of presentation, there is marked variability in the clinical presentation and disease course. Highest mortality occurs in the first year of life. Over 50% of patients require renal transplantation before the age of 20 years.
There is no clear association between ADPKD and an increased risk of renal cell carcinoma.

ADPKD: Patients with an increased risk of developing ESRD include diagnosis before the age of 30 years (relative risk [RR] 2.3 for men, 3.5 for women), hypertension before the age of 35 years (RR 2.7 for men, 3.6 for women), and men with hematuria before the age of 30 years (RR 2.9).
ARPKD: Neonatal ventilation is a strong predictor of mortality. Side effects of congenital hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension can develop in almost half of the patients.
Consider periodic monitoring of renal function (serum creatinine, glomerular filtration rate, proteinuria) and renal size (on imaging studies).
Monitoring and aggressive management of blood pressure.
Monitoring and management of lipids.

Parents with ADPKD should be informed that each of their child has 1 in 2 risk of inheriting the disease, while the risk for parents with ARPKD is 1 in 4 that each child will have the disease and a 1 in 2 that they will be a carrier.
